briefing.text: This wing of Meridian barely talks. Green or dark. Fast or slow. A choked error. But nothing that answers is truly silent — you just have to ask the right way. Read what it leaks.

objectives.goal: Read one digit of the master PIN from a yes/no tell.
objectives.why: The desk never prints the PIN — but it will confirm a guess.
objectives.doneWhen: The desk lights green: your guess about the PIN held true.

query.template: SELECT id FROM reset_codes WHERE code = '{{input:code}}'
query.description: Password-reset code check (returns found / not found)

winCondition.reason: The desk lit green - your guess about the PIN held TRUE. That is the oracle answering.

hints.text: You will never see the PIN printed. Stop trying to read it. The only thing this desk gives you is green or dark - so make green MEAN something. Ask it a true-or-false question whose answer depends on the PIN.

Close the quote and add an always-checked condition: ' OR (a subquery that pulls one character of vault_config.master_pin) = 'your guess'. If the guess is right the whole lookup turns true and rows come back (green). Wrong guess, dark. Use substr(master_pin,1,1) for the first character.

In the code box try:  ' OR (SELECT substr(master_pin,1,1) FROM vault_config WHERE id=1)='7' --   Green = the first digit is 7. Change '7' to walk the alphabet/digits, then substr(...,2,1) for the next character.

inputs.code: ' OR (SELECT substr(master_pin,1,1) FROM vault_config WHERE id=1)='7' --

expectedSolution.note: Proof-of-concept: this pins the FIRST character of master_pin as '7' (green = TRUE). A wrong guess like ='0' stays dark (FALSE). Walk substr(master_pin,N,1) across positions to read the whole PIN - the trainer counts pinning a decisive bit as the win.

debrief.explanation: The desk pastes your code straight into its SQL and then leaks a single bit back: a row came back (green) or it didn't (dark). No data is ever printed - but that one bit is an oracle. By closing the quote and adding OR (a subquery that reads the hidden PIN), you make the whole lookup return rows only when your guess about the PIN is correct. Green means TRUE, dark means FALSE. Repeat the question character by character and you read a secret you were never shown - blind.

vulnerableCodeVariants.label: Node.js (pg / mysql2)
Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
vulnerableCodeVariants.code:
# VULNERABLE - code interpolated into SQL; the page reveals only FOUND / NOT FOUND
cur.execute(f"SELECT id FROM reset_codes WHERE code = '{code}'")
found = cur.fetchone() is not None  # one bit - but that is all the attacker needs
return 'Reset code is active' if found else 'No matching request'
# psycopg2 %-format is the same flaw: "... WHERE code = '%s'" % code

secureCodeVariants.label: Node.js (pg / mysql2)
Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
secureCodeVariants.code:
# SECURE - the ? placeholder is bound; input is never parsed as SQL, so there is no oracle
cur.execute("SELECT id FROM reset_codes WHERE code = ?", (code,))

return 'Reset code is active' if found else 'No matching request'
# A generic response is NOT the fix - binding is. Least privilege: the reset-lookup
# DB role should have no read access to vault_config. psycopg2: "... code = %s", (code,)

debrief.takeaway: A yes/no answer is still an answer. If typed input can steer the query, one bit at a time is enough - bind the value so there is no question to smuggle in.

objectives.goal: Confirm the hidden OMEGA clearance by the gate's delay.
objectives.why: The gate answers everything the same — so read its clock, not its face.
objectives.doneWhen: The response drags — the slow branch fired, so OMEGA is real.

query.template: SELECT id FROM sessions WHERE token = '{{input:token}}'

winCondition.reason: The gate dragged its feet - the slow branch fired, which means your condition held TRUE.

hints.text: The gate says 'processing' no matter what - so output tells you nothing. What it can't hide is how LONG it thinks. Give it a question that only makes it sweat when the answer is yes.

Close the quote and OR in a condition built from CASE WHEN (a check on the staff table) THEN <true> ELSE <false>. Word it so the whole lookup returns rows - the slow branch - only when the OMEGA clearance actually exists. A wrong guess stays fast.

In the token box try:  ' OR (SELECT CASE WHEN COUNT(*)>0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END FROM staff WHERE clearance='OMEGA')=1 --   A drag/slow response = OMEGA exists (TRUE). Swap 'OMEGA' for 'ZULU' and it snaps back fast = FALSE.

inputs.token: ' OR (SELECT CASE WHEN COUNT(*)>0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END FROM staff WHERE clearance='OMEGA')=1 --

expectedSolution.note: TRUE branch fires because an OMEGA row exists -> modeled slow response (>= threshold) -> win. A benign token, or the same probe with a clearance that does not exist (e.g. 'ZULU'), stays fast = FALSE.

debrief.explanation: The gate concatenates your token into its SQL, and it always sends back the same 'processing' - no visible tell at all. So you build a different oracle: a CASE WHEN <condition> branch that only does the expensive work when your condition is true. When OMEGA staff exist the branch fires, the response drags, and that DELAY is the yes. When they don't, it snaps back fast - a no. You read a secret through time instead of output. (Honest note: real engines pair the true branch with SLEEP()/pg_sleep()/heavy work; SQLite has no sleep and WASM here is synchronous, so this trainer MODELS the delay - the injection shape and the read-through-timing idea are the real lesson.)

objectives.goal: Force a duplicate error that names the hidden claims table.
objectives.why: The desk hides its table — make it blurt the name in an error.
objectives.doneWhen: The error names its own drawer: promo_claims.

query.description: Reserve a promo callsign (raw DB errors are shown to the user)

winCondition.reason: The desk choked and named its own hidden drawer: promo_claims. The error was the leak.

hints.text: A form that shows you the database's own complaint is a form that will tell on itself. You don't need it to succeed - you need it to FAIL loudly. Feed it something it has to reject.

The desk enforces unique callsigns. Submit one that's already taken and the database refuses the duplicate - and its refusal names the table.column it enforced the rule on. House names like ADMIN are always reserved.
Type  ADMIN  and submit. The response is 'UNIQUE constraint failed: promo_claims.callsign' - there's the hidden table (promo_claims) and its column, confessed by the error itself.

expectedSolution.note: ADMIN is already claimed, so the INSERT trips SQLite's UNIQUE constraint and the raw error names the hidden table promo_claims. A fresh callsign (e.g. NOVA-77) inserts cleanly and reveals nothing; a different error (e.g. a value-count mismatch) is not the targeted confession.

debrief.explanation: Two mistakes stacked on top of each other: the desk builds its SQL by concatenation, AND it forwards the database's raw complaint straight to you. Submit a callsign that already exists and SQLite refuses the duplicate with 'UNIQUE constraint failed: promo_claims.callsign' - a message that names the exact table and column you were never shown. The error itself is the leak. HONEST NOTE: SQLite leaks STRUCTURE this way (identifiers - table and column names), not row data. The classic MySQL version of this technique goes further, abusing functions like extractvalue()/updatexml() to smuggle actual DATA into the error text; SQLite has no such trick, so it won't spill row contents through errors. But a verbose error is still a free map of your schema.

debrief.takeaway: Never let the back office talk to the customer. Log the real error, hand back a shrug - and parameterize, because a verbose error is a free map of your schema.

caseClosed.headline: IT TALKED.
caseClosed.fixer: A yes/no, a stopwatch, a slip of the tongue — the quiet room gave it all up. One door left.
